CWE-125.question: Can this function read memory before the start or past the end of a buffer, array or string it accesses?

any: an index, offset or length used to read comes from a parameter, input, loop bound or calculation and is not checked against the buffer's size first
a loop reads with an inclusive bound such as i <= len, or one element beyond the data actually stored
c: memcpy, memcmp, strncpy, strlen or pointer arithmetic reads a length that is not tied to the source buffer's real size
a string is read with strlen or a %s format when it may not be NUL-terminated
rust: get_unchecked, slice::from_raw_parts or raw pointer reads inside unsafe use a length or index that is not validated

any: every read index is checked against the length on all paths before the access
the index is a constant, or is masked or reduced modulo the buffer size
the loop bound is the buffer's own length with an exclusive comparison
c: the length passed to a copy is sizeof the source, or the minimum of both sizes
python: the access is ordinary Python indexing or slicing, which raises or clamps rather than reading outside memory
javascript: the access is ordinary array or string indexing, which yields undefined rather than reading outside memory
rust: the access is safe indexing, get() or an iterator, which is bounds-checked by the language

distinguish_from.CWE-129: the defect is a missing or wrong validation of an index taken from input and the read itself is not shown

CWE-787.question: Can this function write memory before the start or past the end of a buffer, array or string it writes to?

any: an index, offset or length used to write comes from a parameter, input, loop bound or calculation and is not checked against the destination's size first
a loop writes with an inclusive bound such as i <= len, or a terminator is written one past the space allocated
c: strcpy, strcat, sprintf, gets or scanf %s write into a fixed-size buffer without a bound
memcpy, memset or strncpy write a length that is not tied to the destination buffer's real size
an allocation size is computed with arithmetic that can overflow before the buffer is filled
rust: ptr::write, copy_nonoverlapping or set_len inside unsafe use a length or index that is not validated

any: every write index is checked against the destination's capacity on all paths before the access
the index is a constant, or is masked or reduced modulo the buffer size
c: bounded functions such as snprintf or strlcpy receive the destination's real size
the copy length is sizeof the destination, or the minimum of both sizes
python: the write is ordinary Python indexing or slice assignment, which raises or grows the list rather than writing outside memory
javascript: the write is ordinary array indexing, which grows the array rather than writing outside memory
rust: the write is safe indexing, push or extend, which is bounds-checked by the language

distinguish_from.CWE-129: the defect is a missing or wrong validation of an index taken from input and the write itself is not shown

CWE-476.question: Can this function dereference a pointer or reference that may be null at that point?

any: a value that the function itself shows may be null (a lookup result, an optional field, a pointer tested for null elsewhere in the function) is used before or without a null test on that path
c: the result of malloc, calloc, realloc, fopen, getenv, strchr or a similar call that can return NULL is dereferenced without a NULL test
a pointer is tested for NULL after it has already been dereferenced
javascript: a property is read from a value that can be null or undefined, such as a find() or getElementById() result, without a check or optional chaining
python: an attribute or item is taken from a value that can be None, such as re.match() or dict.get() results, without a check
rust: a raw pointer from FFI or ptr::null is dereferenced inside unsafe without an is_null check

any: the pointer is tested for null on every path before each use
the value comes from a source that cannot be null, such as the address of a local or a constructor that throws on failure
the only possible null would come from a caller passing one, and nothing in this function suggests callers do
c: the allocation goes through a wrapper that aborts on failure
javascript: optional chaining (?.) or a nullish default (??) guards the access
rust: the value is a reference, Box or Option handled by match, if let, ? or unwrap_or, which cannot dereference null

distinguish_from.CWE-690: the null comes specifically from an unchecked return value and that is the more precise finding
distinguish_from.CWE-416: the pointer is not null but refers to memory that was already freed

CWE-617.question: Does this function contain an assertion that input from outside the program could make fail, ending the process or request?

any: an assert or abort-on-failure check tests a value that comes from a parameter fed by external input, a file, a network message or user data, and that value is not validated before the assertion
c: assert() or a project assertion macro checks a length, count, index or state read from input
python: assert checks request, file or message content (note that python -O removes these, which is a separate concern)
rust: assert!, panic!, unreachable!, unwrap() or expect() fires on a malformed input value rather than a programming error

any: the assertion checks an internal invariant that only a programming error could violate, such as a pointer the function itself just set
the asserted value has already been validated on every path, with an error returned for bad input
the assertion only exists in debug builds and the same condition is handled at run time
c: static_assert or _Static_assert, which is checked at compile time

distinguish_from.REL-026: the hazard is an unguarded division, dereference or index rather than an assertion

REL-026.question: Does this function perform a division, dereference, index or shift whose operand range it never checks, when that operand comes from outside the function?

any: a divisor taken from a parameter, input, length field or calculation is used with / or % without a non-zero test
a shift count from a parameter or input is not bounded by the operand's width
c: buf[i] or ptr + n uses an index from a message, length field or parameter without a range test
a pointer returned by a lookup or allocation is dereferenced without a NULL test

any: the operand range is proven in the function: a non-zero constant divisor, an index masked to the array size, or a test with an early return on every path
the operation cannot fail in this language, such as Python division, which raises a clean exception
rust: checked_div, checked_shl, get() or safe indexing, which report failure rather than corrupting results

distinguish_from.CWE-369: the only hazard is division by zero and that is the more precise finding
distinguish_from.CWE-476: the only hazard is a null dereference and that is the more precise finding
distinguish_from.CWE-129: the only hazard is an unvalidated array index from input and that is the more precise finding

CWE-777.question: Does this function validate or filter a string with a regular expression that is not anchored at both ends, so extra content before or after the match is accepted?

any: a regular expression used to accept or reject input lacks ^ and $ (or \A and \z) and is applied with a search-style call
an allowlist pattern is anchored at only one end
javascript: RegExp.test() or String.match() validates input with a pattern lacking ^...$
python: re.search() or re.match() is used for validation with no $ or \Z at the end of the pattern

any: the regular expression is used to find, extract or replace text rather than to validate or authorise input
the pattern is anchored at both ends, or applied with a whole-string call
rust: Regex::is_match on a pattern wrapped in ^...$

distinguish_from.CWE-1333: the concern is catastrophic backtracking rather than what the pattern accepts

CWE-367.question: Does this function check the state of a file or other shared resource and then act on it in a separate step, so the state can change in between?

any: a file path is checked (exists, access, stat, permissions, is-symlink) and the same path is then opened, created, deleted or changed by a separate call
c: access() or stat() is followed by open() or fopen() on the same path
python: os.path.exists, os.access or os.path.isfile is followed by open, os.remove or os.rename on the same path
javascript: fs.existsSync or fs.access is followed by fs.open, fs.writeFile or fs.unlink on the same path
rust: Path::exists or fs::metadata is followed by File::create, fs::write or fs::remove_file on the same path

any: the operation is done in one atomic call and its error is handled, such as open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, or create_new(true)
the check is made on an already-open handle (fstat on the descriptor) rather than the path
the resource is private to the process, such as a local variable or an in-memory structure behind a lock held across check and use

distinguish_from.CWE-362: the race is between threads on shared memory rather than a check followed by a use of an external resource

PERF-004.question: Does this function build a string by repeated concatenation inside a loop?

any: inside a loop, a string variable is extended with += or s = s + ... on each iteration
javascript: a string is grown with += across loop iterations that can run many times
python: a str is grown with += in a for or while loop

any: parts are collected into a list or array and joined once after the loop
a builder or buffer is used, such as io.StringIO, a String with push_str, or std::string with reserve and append
the loop has a small fixed number of iterations
rust: push_str or write! onto a String, which grows in amortised constant time

distinguish_from.PERF-006: the cost comes from recomputing the same value on each iteration rather than from copying a growing string

PERF-007.question: Does this function repeatedly test membership or search for keys in a list or array inside a loop, where a set or map would make each lookup constant time?

any: inside a loop, x in list, list.index, Array.includes, indexOf, find or a nested loop searches a sequence that grows with the input
the lookup is against a set, dict, map or hash table
the searched sequence is small and fixed, such as a literal of a few items
the membership test runs once rather than per iteration

distinguish_from.PERF-006: the repeated work is a computation unrelated to searching a sequence
